item.content:encoded:
The postseason begins on September 29, giving teams one day of rest between the end of the regular season and the start of the race. Playoff teams must plan their rotations early have the right pitchers rested and ready for the opening series and the Boston Red Sox have seemingly made their call.
The Red Sox's rotation for their upcoming matchup with the Cleveland Guardians, their second-to-last series of the year, is Payton Tolle in game one, Sonny Gray in game two and Ranger Suarez in game three. That leaves Patrick Sandoval, Jake Bennett and Brayan Bello (or a bullpen game) for the final series against the Chicago Cubs, not necessarily in that order.
Tolle has earned the series-opening start against the New York Yankees. He's posted a 2.36 ERA and 0.88 WHIP with 56 strikeouts over his last seven starts. He's stayed hot despite having 143 innings on his arm this year, and he's gotten even better as the year has gone on.
Tolle has had previous success against the Yankees, including two stellar outings this year. He faced the Yankees in his first big league appearance this year and allowed just one run on three hits with 11 strikeouts and a walk over six innings. Tolle next faced New York on June 26 (one of the games in the four-game sweep that started Boston's historic summer winning streak) and he pitched seven, one-hit innings with seven strikeouts.
Red Sox-Guardians series likely previews Boston's Wild Card rotation with Payton Tolle starting Game 1
Starting Tolle first could set up a battle between two young lefties and Cy Young Award contenders (though it isn't much of a contest) if the Yankees plan to open the series with their ace Cam Schlittler. This might not be the case, though, as New York seems to be setting Gerrit Cole up for the Game 1 start. The Red Sox don't fare as well against right-handed pitching as they do against lefties, with a .712 team OPS against them, and taking Boston off its game will be a high priority for its rival.
Whether the Red Sox win or lose Game 1, Game 2 means everything. With a series loss or a sweep on the line, Boston's ace Gray should take the mound. The 36-year-old Gray has surprised fans everywhere by posting one of the best seasons of his career with the Red Sox and his consistency is unmatched.
Gray has clocked a 2.82 ERA, 1.16 WHIP, 146 strikeouts and 45 walks over 163 innings. Like the Red Sox, the Yankees also don't perform especially well against righty pitching, with a .713 OPS as a club. With a sweep on the line or to stay alive, the veteran Gray is the guy to trust.
In a win-or-go-home Game 3, Suarez deserves Boston's trust. He's gotten back on his feet over the last few weeks following a shaky spell (5.70 ERA in August) after a groin injury. Postseason starts are Suarez's bread and butter — he boasts a 1.48 ERA and 1.06 WHIP over 42.2 frames across seven playoff series — and he's the best choice to keep the Red Sox alive when they're on the brink of elimination.
Boston's rotation has been the biggest strength of the team all season. With these three pitchers, in any order, the Red Sox have good chances to get past the Yankees to advance to the Division Series. But setting the energy with Tolle and having the two veterans follow, as Boston has set things up, makes a lot of sense.

Mexicanos que ya aseguraron su pase a postemporada
La presencia de peloteros mexicanos en las últimas ediciones de los playoffs ha sido constante y este año no será la excepción pues hasta ahorita se tiene confirmada la participación de cuatro peloteros mexicanos y dos con estatus todavía pendiente, ya que uno está en sucursales y el otro se encuentra en lista de lesionados.

A continuación, te presentamos la lista de jugadores nacionales que estarán en los playoffs:
Jonathan Aranda (Tampa Bay Rays)
Ha firmado su campaña más sólida y consagratoria en MLB. Con 149 juegos jugados, el infielder presume un promedio de bateo de .277, conectando 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y remolcando 92 carreras, convirtiéndose en una pieza medular en el lineup de los Rays.
Jarren Durán (Boston Red Sox):
Se ha consolidado como un auténtico motor en los senderos y el jardín central. A lo largo de la temporada suma 20 jonrones, 69 carreras impulsadas y 19 bases robadas en 145 encuentros, destacando además por su velocidad con 5 triples.

Joey Ortiz (Milwaukee Brewers):
Ha sido una de las grandes revelaciones del año tras su llegada a Milwaukee, aportando una defensa de élite en el cuadro y un bateo sumamente oportuno que ayudó a los Brewers a amarrar temprano su boleto a octubre.
Patrick Sandoval (Boston Red Sox):
El lanzador que representó a México en el Clásico Mundial de Beisbol regresó esta temporada tras un periodo largo fuera de las canchas y ha tenido altibajos con los Boston Red Sox con una efectividad de 5.15 y un récord de 1-7.
Manuel Rodríguez (Tampa Bay Rays):
El lanzador yucateco venía sumando valiosos relevos con efectividad de 3.86 y 8 ponches en el bullpen de Tampa Bay en los cuatro juegos que disputó.

Alek Thomas (Oklahoma City Comets):
Después de haber sido cambiado desde los Arizona Diamondbacks a inicios de año, el jardinero Alek Thomas se encuentra actualmente en las sucursales de Los Angeles Dodgers
Aunque tuvo una breve participación de 7 juegos con el primer equipo de los Dodgers bateando para .211, la tremenda profundidad del roster angelino ha hecho que se mantenga buscando ritmo en el sistema de ligas menores, a la espera de un llamado que lo devuelva al roster de postemporada.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are headed back to the postseason, but their work is not finished. Boston enters the final week of the regular season at 84-72 after Sunday’s 5-1 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. The Red Sox secured their second consecutive postseason appearance when other results around the American League eliminated the remaining path for them to fall out of the playoff field.
The final six games will determine how prepared Boston looks when October begins. All six will be played at Fenway Park.
The Red Sox host the Cleveland Guardians at 6:45 p.m. ET on Tuesday, 7:10 p.m. Wednesday and 6:45 p.m. Thursday. Boston will conclude the regular season with three games against the Chicago Cubs from Friday through Sunday. Cleveland arrives with its own postseason urgency. The Guardians are attempting to protect their position from the Chicago White Sox, who remain close behind in the standings.
The Cubs enter the week at 87-69 after defeating the Cincinnati Reds 9-1. Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run Sunday and has emerged as one of the most dangerous power-speed players in the National League.
Trying To Get Right With The Bats
Boston’s most immediate assignment is restoring its offense. The Red Sox managed only six hits during Sunday’s loss to Tampa Bay. Trevor Story prevented a shutout with a ninth-inning home run, but Boston wasted its best opportunity after loading the bases in the fifth inning.
Roman Anthony struck out to end that threat. Patrick Sandoval allowed five runs, although he recovered from a four-run first inning to complete seven frames. The loss dropped Boston to 84-72.
Chad Tracy must use the final week to balance two priorities.
The Red Sox need enough intensity to sharpen their offense and settle any remaining pitching questions. They also cannot afford to exhaust or injure important players immediately before the postseason.
Bullpen Questions
The bullpen hierarchy is another issue. Close games against Cleveland and Chicago can function as postseason rehearsals, allowing Tracy to test his preferred late-inning combinations before every decision becomes potentially season-ending.
The Red Sox cannot catch Tampa Bay in the American League East, and the New York Yankees remain ahead of Boston in second place. That makes the final six games less about chasing a division championship and more about playoff positioning, health and momentum.
Boston already possesses its October invitation. The final week will determine what kind of team arrives.

ST. PETERSBURG -- After finishing their regular-season home schedule with yet another victory at Tropicana Field, the Rays are potentially one win away from clinching their first American League East championship since 2021.
The Rays jumped out to a big lead against the Red Sox in Sunday afternoon’s series finale and rolled to a 5-1 win, their 55th of the season in their rebuilt and restored home dome. That capped an 8-1 homestand with three walk-off victories and three straight series victories against the Astros, A’s and Red Sox, who clinched a spot in the postseason before leaving town anyway thanks to Houston’s loss to Atlanta.
“They're all big, but today was big -- and just incredibly impressed with the way the guys have gone about their business,” manager Kevin Cash said. “We knew this was going to be a big homestand, and they played extremely well.”
The Yankees’ 8-4 loss to the D-backs on Sunday afternoon extended the Rays’ division lead to six games with seven left to play. Tampa Bay only needs to win one game in the four-game series at Yankee Stadium that starts with a doubleheader on Tuesday to officially wrap up the top seed in the league.
“This month hasn't been easy by any terms. Been playing teams either in the playoffs or fighting for playoff spots. So it's been a dogfight this month,” starter Nick Martinez said. “I think we just did a good job of staying focused on what we do best and keeping our eyes ahead.”
Before flying to New York, they had to finish the home portion of their regular-season schedule on a similarly high note as they moved a season-high 35 games over .500 at 95-60.
The Rays put together a 55-26 record at the Trop this season, the third-highest home winning percentage in franchise history behind 2008 (57-24, .704) and the pandemic-shortened 2020 campaign (20-9, .690). Three of their “home” wins in ‘08 came at Disney’s Wide World of Sports, so they actually set a franchise record this season by winning 55 games at the Trop.
Tampa Bay’s players, coaches and staff knew they would appreciate being back in their longtime home ballpark this season after spending last year playing outdoors at George M. Steinbrenner Field after the Trop was damaged by Hurricane Milton. They showed it on the field all season, and they’ll get more opportunities to display their home-field advantage in the postseason.
“I think after last year, we kind of missed this place,” outfielder Jonny DeLuca said.
What has made Tropicana Field such a welcome home for these Rays? Jax pointed out that visitors typically aren’t comfortable underneath the Trop’s tilted roof, unaccustomed to the turf, the catwalks and everything else that makes this place unique.
“I think just the fact that a lot of other teams with 'natural' stadiums didn't want to play here, and us embracing that, everything that the city and the stadium just went through, and just making it our home,” left fielder Chandler Simpson added. “I feel like we're a scrappy, get-our-hands-dirty type of team, and I feel like the stadium fits that.”
Of course, the Rays have proven they can win just about anywhere when they play the kind of game they did in Sunday’s finale.
The Rays’ first three batters loaded the bases against Red Sox lefty Patrick Sandoval, then DeLuca drove in two of them with a double to left. Junior Caminero and DeLuca immediately scored on a single by Simpson, giving Tampa Bay’s pitching staff a sizable lead.
That was the first time since May 18, 2022, that the Rays’ first five batters reached consecutively to begin the game, and Victor Mesa Jr. added to their advantage in the fourth by ripping his 14th homer of the season out to right field.
“It's a bunch of good at-bats that we can string together from one to nine in our lineup, and they just continue to put pressure on pitchers,” Cash said. “Then we've got the right guys to come through in those moments.”
Jax hardly needed that kind of breathing room, as he struck out five over five scoreless innings, giving him a 0.60 ERA in three starts since Sept. 9. He ran into one jam in the fifth, loading the bases with two outs, but struck out Roman Anthony to finish another strong performance.
Next stop: New York. Next celebration: Tuesday?
“We knew what we had to do,” Jax said. “We wanted to put ourselves in a good place going into New York, make it a little bit easier.”

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay Rays crept closer to the AL East title with a 5-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Sunday.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Despite the loss, the Red Sox later secured a playoff berth when the Houston Astros lost to the Atlanta Braves. The Red Sox waited out the Astros-Braves result and held a celebration in their clubhouse. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
Sandoval then retired 21 of his next 23 batters and worked through the seventh inning, allowing only a first-inning walk and a fourth-inning homer, both to Victor Mesa Jr.
Up next
After a day off Monday, Boston will start LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.02) at home against the Cleveland Guardians. Right-hander Nick Martinez (15-4, 2.94) is set to start the opener of the doubleheader in New York, while right-hander Drew Rasmussen (15-5, 2.72) to pitch Game 2.

AL-best Rays complete 8-1 homestand by stifling Red Sox
(Photo credit: Pablo Robles)
Tampa Bay's Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson drove in a pair apiece in a four-run first inning, Victor Mesa Jr. homered and the Rays won for the eighth time in their final regular-season homestand by beating the Boston Red Sox 5-1 on Sunday afternoon in St. Petersburg, Fla.
In finishing 8-1 on their last homestand before the postseason, the Rays (95-60) sent nine batters to the plate in the first and never looked back as they concluded their home schedule with a majors-best 55-26 mark.
Starter Griffin Jax (8-10) fired five scoreless frames with three hits allowed. He fanned five with two walks over 74 offerings.
Trevor Story homered, and Roman Anthony (double) and Caleb Durbin each went 2-for-4. However, Boston (84-72) managed only six hits in losing its second straight.
Starter Patrick Sandoval (1-7) rebounded from a terrible beginning to finish seven innings, allowing five runs on four hits. He struck out five, walked two and hit a batter in 94 pitches.
Tampa Bay put its first five batters on base against Sandoval, and DeLuca doubled in two runs before Simpson singled in two more as the Rays batted around in the first.
Jax was dialed in early after yielding a leadoff single to Anthony. The right-hander retired 10 straight batters, four by strikeouts, until Adley Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth.
In the bottom of the fourth, Mesa made it 5-0 by cranking Sandoval's 95 mph four-seamer out to right-center a Statcast-estimated 403 feet. It was the right fielder's 14th home run.
The Red Sox had a chance to get back in it by loading the bases in the fifth on a single by Durbin and two walks, but Anthony -- who drove in five of the club's six runs in the series -- whiffed to end it on a sinking 2-2 changeup from Jax, the starter's final pitch.
With a fire alarm going off behind center field causing a short delay, Cole Sulser tossed a perfect sixth as the bullpen began its stretch of four innings of one-run work.
Story hit his fifth homer with one out in the ninth to spoil the shutout.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways.
They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs.
A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on back-to-back two-run base hits by centerfielder Jonny DeLuca (double) and left-fielder Chandler Simpson (single) before the Red Sox starter could record an out. Sandoval issued his second walk of the inning to Victor Mesa Jr. before he finished the frame and stranded two runners.
“Nightmare, like legit nightmare situation,” a grimacing Sandoval told reporters postgame of the first inning. “Couldn’t really where my arm was in space, grip on the ball wasn’t great. Just a literal nightmare.”
Then came a complete 180. Sandoval looked like a new man when he returned for the bottom of the second. He set the Rays down in order on eight pitches, then needed six to do so again in the third.
Sandoval retired eight consecutive Rays before Mesa homered with one out in the fourth to push the lead to five. But it marked Tampa Bay’s fourth and final hit of the day; Sandoval retired his last 11 batters, and newly-returned righty Tyron Guerrero extended the streak to 14 with a 1-2-3 eighth.
Yet the Red Sox, who left 17 men on base over the first two games of the series, were blanked by righty Griffin Jax and the Rays bullpen until a brief rally bid in the top of the ninth. Boston out-hit Tampa Bay 6-4, but went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position, and stranded six.
Roman Anthony led off the game with a groundball single to right, but he was erased and replaced when catcher Adley Rutschman popped into a force out. The Red Sox did not put another man on base until Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth, an opportunity quickly erased by shortstop Trevor Story grounding into an inning-ending double play.
Boston’s best chance came and went in Jax’s fifth and final frame, when they loaded the bases on a one-out single by third baseman Caleb Durbin, and walks to centerfielder Jarren Duran and right-fielder Nate Eaton. Jax, who had not exceeded 67 pitches in a start since Aug. 2, was up to 69 when Anthony came to bat with two outs and the bases loaded. It took five pitches to end the threat; Anthony swung and missed at Jax’s last two, a 95.3 mph sinker and 90.2 mph changeup.
Much like Saturday’s 2-1 loss, Boston had no hope against the Tampa Bay bullpen. The Red Sox went in order against Cole Sulser in the sixth, and Brody Hopkins in the seventh.
Facing 2025 Red Sox trade deadline acquisition Steven Matz in the eighth, Anthony doubled with two outs. Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for designated hitter Mickey Gasper. Jones has dominated left-handed pitching since the Red Sox acquired him from the Detroit Tigers during the All-Star break, but Matz struck him out swinging on four pitches.
After his 40-pitch first, Sandoval completed his remaining six innings on a mere 54. He became just the fourth Red Sox pitcher in the last 26 years, and first since Rick Porcello in 2016, to pitch at least seven innings after giving up at least four runs in the first. Sandoval yielded five earned runs on four hits, walked two (both in the first), and struck out five over seven innings. He threw 73.4% of his 94 pitches for strikes.
Activated from the injured list Sunday morning, Guerrero was sharp in his first inning of work since Aug. 31. The towering righty retired the Rays’ No. 2-4 batters, including American League home-run leader Junior Caminero, in order on 12 pitches (nine strikes). Guerrero’s return will bolster a Boston bullpen currently without closer Aroldis Chapman (day-to-day with lat tightness), and righty Justin Slaten (season-ending flexor injury).
Story ensured the Red Sox would not be shut out. His fifth home run of the year, off righty Ty Johnson, soared 405 feet to left at 102.7 mph with one out in the ninth.
Thus concludes the final Red Sox road trip of the season. They went 2-4 against the Texas Rangers and Rays, were outscored 23-15, and left 42 men on base.
After an off-day Monday, their final homestand of the season begins Tuesday night against the Cleveland Guardians.
But first, all eyes turn to the Braves and Astros.

Boston Red Sox right-hander Kutter Crawford was set to make a rehab start with Triple-A Worcester. But with the game being cancelled due to rain, per the Worcester Telegram-Gazette's Tommy Cassell, the club faces a tough roster decision on the 30-year-old starter.
The cancellation also ends Worcester's season. That means the Red Sox will have to decide if they want to roster Crawford during the final seven games of the regular season, and possibly the postseason.
Crawford is currently on the 60-day injured list after suffering a major setback in his recovery from wrist surgery. After a rehab start in April, he experienced issues in his right elbow and has been shelved since. This appearance would have been his first outing in five months.
Red Sox Face Tough Roster Decision on Kutter Crawford
With nowhere to get a rehab outing, the Red Sox will have to decide the next steps for Kutter Crawford. They certainly had some contingency in place if the game was affected by weather.
The first question the Red Sox have to answer is whether Crawford is an option for the postseason. If not, they will likely just shut him down. Otherwise, they have to clear a 40-man roster spot to activate him from the injured list.
If Boston does roster the 30-year-old, it will likely be in a relief role. The Red Sox will likely go into the Wild Card Series with a three-man rotation of Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, and Payton Tolle. If they advance further, they could turn to either Jake Bennett or Brayan Bello as their fourth starter.
Given the postseason in general, there could be some need for an innings-eater for the bullpen. But Bello and Bennett are further stretched out than Crawford at this point in the season.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Red Sox have been unerringly diligent about resting players as they prepare for the postseason. But they still haven’t clinched their spot.
They slept through a 5-1 loss against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field on Sunday, managing only six hits before a crowd of 24,654.
The Sox left the field needing the Braves to beat the Astros to finally clinch their spot.
It has been a slog for a while. The Sox were 2-4 on their road trip and are 11-13 since Aug. 26. They end the regular season with a six-game homestand starting Tuesday against the Guardians.
The Sox scored two runs in the last two games against the Rays and were 1 for 15 with runners in scoring position, leaving 14 men on base.
Griffin Jax (8-10) and five relievers allowed six hits on Sunday. The Sox had a chance to get back in the game in the fifth inning when they loaded the bases with two outs, but Roman Anthony struck out.
Patrick Sandoval (1-7) allowed four runs during a 40-pitch first inning.
The lefthander walked Yandy Díaz on four pitches, then hit Ryan Vilade with a 2-and-2 fastball. Junior Caminero singled to left field to load the bases.
Jonny DeLuca followed with a two-run double to left and Chandler Simpson with a two-run single to right. That was essentially the game as the Sox could not punch back until Trevor Story had a solo home run off Ty Johnson in the ninth inning.
Sandoval completed seven innings and allowed only one more run, on a home run by Victor Mesa Jr. After the long first inning, Sandoval threw 54 pitches over the next six and faced only 19 batters.

'We've had some big performances. I feel like it's a different guy every night,' said Jones, who notched his sixth homer of the season in a night in which Roman Anthony went deep and had three RBIs.
'Everybody in here knows what we're playing for. I feel we've had a lot of tight ball games. That last one in Texas (on Thursday) and then (Friday showed) who we are and what our baseball is.'
The Red Sox (84-71) saw their momentum slowed on Saturday, however, with a 2-1 setback to the Rays (94-60). They enter the game comfortably in line for the second wild card in the American League.
Richie Palacios had an RBI single in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero with the winning run. It marked the third walk-off win of the season-ending homestand for Tampa Bay.
'We're just relentless. No matter what's going on in the game, we always feel like we have a chance to win,' Palacios said. 'Three walk-offs is amazing, and we're just going to continue to do what we do.'

'It's very encouraging. It's a good feeling,' Rays manager Kevin Cash said following Saturday's game. 'You want to get as many reps at that as possible, because we know the games that we're going to continue playing this year are going to be against good teams and in tight ballgames.'

The Boston Red Sox and Tampa Bay Rays head into Sunday’s series finale at Fenway Park with the three-game set knotted at one win apiece after Saturday’s 2-1 Rays victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval takes the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax, a matchup that carries extra weight with the regular season winding down and playoff positioning still in flux.
Interim manager Chad Tracy has kept the bulk of his starting nine intact, but he has made a modest yet noticeable adjustment involving outfielder Jarren Duran, via Underdog MLB.
After sitting out the series opener and batting eighth on Saturday, Duran will slide up one spot into the seventh hole. He will hit in front of Isaiah Kiner-Falefa and Nate Eaton while remaining in center field, the position he has occupied since injuries to Ceddanne Rafaela and Eli White opened the job.
The rest of the order features Roman Anthony in left, Mickey Gasper at designated hitter, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Trevor Story at shortstop, Nick Sogard at first, and Cooper Durbin at third.
The move comes during a difficult individual season for Duran. Entering Sunday he is hitting .206 in 144 games, with 65 runs, 110 hits, 20 home runs and 69 RBIs. His slugging percentage sits at .364 and his OPS at .626.
Speculation about a possible trade lingered for weeks before the August 4 deadline, yet Duran remained in a Red Sox uniform and has continued to receive regular playing time as the club pushes toward October.
Boston sits at 84-71 with seven games left and occupies what currently looks like the second American League Wild Card spot. Should the standings hold, the Red Sox would open the postseason on the road in a best-of-three Wild Card series against the New York Yankees.
Every remaining game, including Sunday’s finale against a familiar division rival, therefore carries playoff implications.
Tracy’s decision to bump Duran up in the order is a small tactical shift rather than a wholesale overhaul, but it signals a willingness to tinker as the club tries to generate more consistent offense down the stretch.
Whether the extra spot in the lineup produces results remains to be seen.
Duran’s season-long struggles have been well documented, yet he has shown flashes of the power and speed that once made him a fixture in the middle of Boston’s order.
A productive afternoon against Jax and the Rays would give the Red Sox a series victory and a bit of momentum heading into the final week.
With the calendar now late September and the postseason picture still taking shape, even incremental lineup changes can feel significant.

The Boston Red Sox roster is about to get a bit more crowded as several players are set to return from the injured list before the end of the season. Additionally, even some players who make the cut and play in October might find themselves looking for new homes this winter for a variety of reasons.
One thing the Red Sox have is a solid amount of depth. It's what allowed the club to survive so many injuries and mount a rally after such a horrendous start to the season.
On the flip side, sometimes too much depth is a bad thing. There are only so many roster spots to go around, and at a certain point, Boston needs impact players and not just guys who can hold down the fort in case of emergency.
5 players who are entering their final days as a member of the Red Sox
Masataka Yoshida
We'll start with a controversial one. Getting rid of Masataka Yoshida outright would mean eating $18 million in 2027. Even moving him in a trade would likely result in the Red Sox paying down a good portion of his contract. That doesn't exactly sound like something John Henry would go for.
However, there are just too many reasons why the 33-year-old is no longer worth a roster spot. Injuries have played a major role in Yoshida's Red Sox career. On top of that, it's hard to justify a platoon DH without much power and no defensive ability taking up a roster spot, especially given Boston's outfield logjam. There's a chance he's back from the IL prior to the playoffs starting, but it's hard to see how he fits the postseason roster.
Patrick Sandoval
Patrick Sandoval was a worthwhile dart throw as an injury stash when the Red Sox signed him ahead of the 2025 season. With that said, he's shown that he's not much more than a fifth starter at this point. Boston has an abundance of pitching depth, especially of the left-handed variety, making it a near-certainty that the free-agent-to-be is seeking employment elsewhere this offseason.
Isiah Kiner-Falefa
This is a tough one because, in many ways, Isiah Kiner-Falefa has exceeded expectations this season. The utility infielder is having a career season at the plate and has been a spark plug for Boston. However, does his value hold up as well if his bat falls off more in line with his career averages? There is some intangible value to keeping him around, but it's hard to pony up for a cheerleader when the club has other younger and cheaper options.
Triston Casas
Not technically in a Red Sox uniform due to his litany of injuries, but it's fair to say that Triston Casas' days as a member of the organization are numbered. He can't be counted on to stay healthy. It's unclear what his production would look like after so much time away. Finally, Boston could really do without the headaches. This is a clear non-tender case.
Jahmai Jones
It's starting to become clear why Jahmai Jones never got much of an opportunity to carve out a big league role before 2025. Jones is supposed to mash lefties while playing some outfield and DHing, but for much of the season he's done nothing of the sort. Even his breakout 2025 campaign came over just 150 plate appearances. It's not exactly worth going into arbitration with a player who's failing at executing the one skill he supposedly has.

Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

Sep 20, 2026, 12:47 AM ET
WEEI's Rob Bradford reports that it is "sure looking like" Boston Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle has a "good shot" at pitching Game 1 of a wild-card series to kick off the postseason with the way the Red Sox are lining things up. It means that the 23-year-old southpaw will not get a start this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays. The former second-rounder from TCU in 2024 has had a strong first full season in the big leagues with Boston in 2026, going 9-6 with a 3.02 ERA (3.04 FIP) and 1.07 WHIP with 166 strikeouts and 38 walks in 143 innings across his 25 starts. Another lefty, Patrick Sandoval, is now scheduled to make the start for the BoSox in the series finale in Tampa. Tolle allowed four earned runs in 5 2/3 innings against the Seattle Mariners on Aug. 31, but he has only given up one earned run with one walk and 19 punchouts in 12 innings across his last two starts against the Baltimore Orioles and Kansas City Royals in September.--Keith Hernandez
Source: WEEI - Rob Bradford

Xavier Edwards Leaves Early on Saturday With Thumb Discomfort


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:31 AM ET
Miami Marlins infielder Xavier Edwards (thumb) left Saturday night's game at Petco Park against the San Diego Padres early with discomfort in his left thumb, according to Christina De Nicola. The Marlins' training staff was checking Edwards' left hand out when he fouled a ball off in the seventh frame. It is worth noting that Edwards previously missed time this season with a sprained left thumb, which he might have aggravated on Saturday night. Before leaving the ballgame, Edwards went 0-for-3 with a walk and two strikeouts. He was replaced at the keystone in San Diego by Jared Serna. If the 27-year-old switch-hitting middle infielder did aggravate his left-thumb sprain, there is a good chance that he will not play again for the Marlins in the final week of the 2026 season. Edwards came into Wednesday's contest with a nice .282/.361/.373 slash line with a .733 OPS, a career-high six home runs, a career-high 52 RBI, 61 runs scored, and 21 stolen bases in 141 games played. He has stolen 20-plus bases in each of the last three seasons, including a career-high 31 back in 2024.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Aaron Judge Hopes to be Back for Postseason, No Timetable Given


Keith Hernandez




Sep 20, 2026, 12:23 AM ET
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge (calf) said on Saturday that his right-calf strain is in the soleus muscle, according to Bryan Hoch of MLB.com. However, Judge would not say what grade of strain his MRI exam revealed. "I'd like to be back by the postseason. That's definitely the plan. I got really no answers for you on any timeline or anything like that," Judge said. The New York Daily News' Gary Phillips reports that neither Judge nor manager Aaron Boone has shared much information on his injury, with the Yankees treating his calf strain like "classified CIA intel." "It doesn't matter what grade it is," Boone said. "We're at nine games left [in the season]." Because we have no idea of the exact severity of his calf injury, it is entirely plausible that Judge could miss most, or all, of any potential Yankees playoff run in October. Judge has been throwing, working out, and getting treatment, and he said he is "gonna do everything we can do to get back as soon as we can." Boone, though, merely said he is "hoping for the best." It will be difficult for the Yankees to go all the way if they do not get Judge back for the playoffs. It has been a frustrating year for the three-time MVP and all of his fantasy managers, as he has only played in 66 games due to a stress fracture in his rib, slashing .241/.360/.511 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI, 45 runs, and five steals.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Bryan Hoch

Sep 19, 2026, 10:37 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher Roki Sasaki (finger) will make his return to the mound next week during the series against the San Diego Padres, David Vassegh reports. It doesn't sound like the Dodgers have decided whether Sasaki will start or come out of the bullpen during his outing against the Padres. He only made one rehab appearance at Triple-A Buffalo before getting cleared to pitch for the big league club. The Jays plan to have Yesavage pitch roughly three innings or around 45 to 50 pitches. Spencer Miles is expected to take over for the bulk of the innings after Yesavage is done. It'll be interesting to see if the Jays decide to shut down Yesavage if they do get eliminated from playoff contention. Texas Rangers starting pitcher Cal Quantrill (lat) exited early during Saturday's outing against the Toronto Blue Jays. Jones is 1-for-19 with nine strikeouts over his last four games, so he could probably use a day off to rest and reset. Jose Caballero takes over in center field for Saturday's game. The Dodgers have already clinched the postseason, so they don't exactly need to rush him back into the lineup. However, the Dodgers would probably like for Ohtani to play in a few regular-season games before the playoffs begin. Fantasy managers should check back for another update in a few days.--Andy Webb
Source: Jack Harris

Sep 19, 2026, 5:54 PM ET
Kansas City Royals first baseman/outfielder Jac Caglianone (hand) is serving as the designated hitter and is batting third in Saturday's contest on the road against the Pittsburgh Pirates and right-hander Bubba Chandler, per MLB.com. Caglianone suffered a minor hand injury before Friday's series opener at PNC Park, but he is back in action on Saturday and should be returned to fantasy lineups against a right-hander, despite his cold streak of late. The 23-year-old former first-rounder has produced a .277/.328/.483 slash line with an .811 OPS, 23 home runs, 70 RBI, 66 runs scored, and six stolen bases in 484 at-bats in 2026 in his first full big-league season with the Royals. Cags was red-hot in August, slashing .411/.429/.684 with a 1.113 OPS, six home runs, eight doubles, 26 RBI, 17 runs scored, and three stolen bases in 24 games, but he has been banged up in September and has gone just 4-for-27 (.148) with zero homers, four RBI, one walk, and 11 strikeouts. He has never faced Chandler in the majors.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Sebastian Walcott to be Promoted to Triple-A


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 3:01 PM ET
Texas Rangers top infield prospect Sebastian Walcott is expected to be promoted to Triple-A Round Rock on Saturday, according to Kennedi Landry of MLB.com. Walcott will make his debut as the designated hitter on Saturday night. The No. 9 overall prospect in all of baseball, per MLB Pipeline, has only played in 39 games in the minors this year after having surgery on his UCL, but since returning, he has slashed .322/.398/.586 with nine home runs and 11 stolen bases in 37 games for Double-A Frisco. In a playoff series with the Rough Riders, Walcott went 4-for-11 with a homer and four stolen bases. Walcott is only 20 years old, but if he continues to ascend and looks good in spring training next year, he could push for an early-season MLB promotion for the Rangers. It is impossible to ignore his 40-homer upside at the shortstop position in fantasy baseball, which makes him a must-stash already in dynasty/keeper leagues.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Kennedi Landry
Orioles Shutting Ryan Helsley Down


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:40 PM ET
The Baltimore Orioles are shutting down right-handed reliever Ryan Helsley (elbow) for the rest of the season, general manager Mike Elias told Andy Kostka of The Baltimore Banner. The focus is on Helsley getting ready for next season. Elias said that Helsley is not dealing with a new injury, but the debate was over contracting his buildup timeline, and the O's opted against that. In related news, the Orioles reinstated right-handed reliever Felix Bautista (shoulder) from the 60-day injured list, and he will join the team's active roster for the first time since July of last year after he had surgery to fix a torn labrum and rotator cuff in his shoulder. Helsley's first year in Baltimore was a lost cause due to his elbow issues, as he was able to throw only 15 1/3 innings, going 0-4 with a 4.11 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 21 strikeouts, and eight saves in 17 appearances. He will not be a lock to open the 2027 campaign as Baltimore's primary closer, especially with Bautista now back and healthy.--Keith Hernandez

Willson Contreras Still Out on Saturday


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 1:04 PM ET
Boston Red Sox first baseman Willson Contreras (hand) remains out of the team's starting lineup for Saturday's contest against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays for the second straight day, per MLB.com. Nick Sogard will make another start at first base and will bat fifth against Rays right-hander Freddy Peralta. Contreras was diagnosed with a bruised right hand after leaving Thursday's game against the Texas Rangers after he was hit by a pitch. X-rays came back negative, though, so he is considered day-to-day and could make his return in Sunday's series finale in Tampa. Fantasy managers are hoping to get the 34-year-old Venezuelan back in their starting lineups as soon as possible, as the four-time All-Star has hit a career-high 27 home runs while driving in 81 runs in 129 games and 533 plate appearances in his first year with the club. Various injuries have limited Contreras to only four games so far in September, though, and he has gone 4-for-12 with a homer and two RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com
Aroldis Chapman Won't Pitch This Weekend


Keith Hernandez




Sep 19, 2026, 11:07 AM ET
Boston Red Sox left-handed closer Aroldis Chapman (lat) felt some tightness in his lat while working out before Tuesday's game against the Texas Rangers and has not pitched since. Chapman said that he will not pitch this weekend against the division-rival Tampa Bay Rays, but he expects to return during the final homestand of the regular season, which starts on Tuesday, according to Ian Browne of MLB.com. The veteran southpaw downplayed the injury on Friday, saying that the Red Sox are being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the series opener against the Rays, but the team told him not to. "I'm not worried at all," Chapman said. "From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time." Fantasy managers will be without Chapman this weekend, but for championship matchups next week, he will hopefully be ready to return to ninth-inning duties. The 38-year-old has been excellent in 2026 in his second year in Boston, posting a 1.95 ERA with a 1.14 WHIP, 34 saves, and 68 strikeouts in 50 2/3 innings pitched. Source: MLB.com - Ian Browne

Despite that, Ashcraft is unlikely to make enough progress to get back on the mound before the end of the regular season. Ashcraft has been out since early September due to right arm discomfort. Ashcraft is probably done for the year, but he did post a breakout campaign for the Pirates this season. Across 28 starts, Ashcraft posted a 3.65 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, and a 173/35 K/BB ratio across 165.1 innings of work.--Andy Webb

The Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) defeated the Boston Red Sox (84-71) 2-1 on Saturday evening at Tropicana Field. With the win, the Rays have evened the three-game series as they continue a push to try to win the American League East crown.
The Red Sox got on the board in the third inning thanks to a RBI double from Roman Anthony. In the bottom of the fourth, Jonathan Aranda hit a solo homer to tie the game 1-1. That would remain the score until the bottom of the ninth inning.
Junior Caminero led off the bottom of the ninth with a single to left, before Jonny DeLuca popped out. Chandler Simpson then hit a single to put runners on first and second, before those runners both advanced thanks to a passed ball from Red Sox catcher Connor Wong. Victor Mesa Jr then struck out before Richie Palacios came to the plate. With runners on second and third and two outs, Palacios singled on a shallow fly ball to right field that fell in and allowed the Rays to leave Tropicana Field as walk-off winners.
Freddy Peralta got the start and allowed just one earned run on four hits in five and two-third innings of work in which he struck out six and walked two. Bryan Baker (4-2, 1.49) picked up the win out of the bullpen after working a scoreless top of the ninth inning.
The Rays will now try to win the series against the Red Sox when they meet in the finale on Sunday afternoon. Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80) is scheduled to start for the Rays and face Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) for the Red Sox. First pitch on Sunday is scheduled for 1:40 PM - pregame coverage begins at 1:00 PM on 95.7 WDAE.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

The Boston Red Sox probably won't get a full sense of their 2026 trade deadline performance this season, despite the positive injury updates on Curtis Mead. The former Washington National will hit off a tee in the coming days — his first offensive progress since he succumbed to a wrist injury during his Red Sox debut — but there's a good chance he doesn't progress fast enough to return this year.
On the other hand, the Nationals will soon get a look at their return from the trade, Connelly Early. The young lefty was on the injured list with elbow inflammation when the Nats traded for him on July 26. He's recently taken some major steps in his rehab.
Washington on September 13 sent Early on a rehab assignment. In one inning with the Triple-A Rochester Red Wings, he allowed three runs on two hits and two walks with two strikeouts.
Nationals President of Baseball Operations (and former Red Sox Assistant General Manager) Paul Toboni confirmed on "The Sports Junkies" show on 106.7 The Fan that Early will make another rehab appearance on September 20 before he makes his DC debut on September 26 against the New York Mets. The season ends on September 28, so Washington will get a look at Early in the major leagues just in time.
Nationals confirm former Red Sox pitcher Connelly Early will make first big league start since trade on September 26
The Nationals were eliminated from playoff contention over the weekend, which could be one reason they're letting Early start. It's already been over two months since the rookie last pitched, but there's no stakes on getting a preview of Early's talent.
Early posted a 3.44 ERA, 1.25 WHIP, 93 strikeouts and 34 walks over 91.2 innings with the Red Sox this season. Washington's rotation hasn't looked sharp lately, despite Cade Cavalli's utter dominance since he faced the Red Sox on June 30 (2.27 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 112 strikeouts over his last 15 games). Early will be an upgrade over Jake Irvin (5.51 ERA in 96.1 innings) or rookie Jackson Kent (6.40 ERA in 32.1 innings), who has only pitched a tiny sample size of innings, but they haven't been good.
The Red Sox's rotation could use another arm given Patrick Sandoval and Jake Bennett's recent struggles, but holding onto Early wouldn't have done much for them given his long IL stint during the playoff race. Boston dealt from a position of depth to acquire Mead and it deserves credit for doing so despite the unfortunate circumstances that led to his placement on the IL.
Just in the nick of time, the Nationals will get to see what Early can do on the mound before the season ends. The Red Sox may not get so lucky with Mead, even though their season will continue into October.

item.content:encoded:
The regular season is rapidly coming to an end, and the Boston Red Sox still don't have ace pitcher Garrett Crochet back. That could be changing soon, though.
It had previously been reported that Crochet was set to return for the first round of the playoffs. Now, Chris Cotillo of MassLive noted in a report that the Red Sox may be pushing to have Crochet pitch in the regular season. This would act as a kind of rehab outing.
"The comebacks of potential October contributors like Tanner Houck, Garrett Crochet, Johan Oviedo and others might also be aided by the fact the Red Sox might have a week (or more) to set up for the postseason," Cotillo wrote. "It's not out of the question that the club has someone like Crochet pitch in one of the final regular season games of the year in what's effectively a rehab outing at the major league level in a game that matters little in the standings."
After finishing second in AL Cy Young voting in 2025, 2026 has been a major disappointment for Crochet. He has a 6.30 ERA and hasn't pitched since April 29th, when he originally hit the IL with left shoulder inflammation. He would later also be diagnosed with a lat strain.
When Crochet does return, it won't be in the rotation. He doesn't have time to build up to that. Instead, the Red Sox are going to be using him out of the bullpen. he
Boston Red Sox Ace Garrett Crochet Doesn't Have Time for a Rehab
The reality for Garrett Crochet is that time is running out for a rehab assignment, and he likely won't have time to make one. That's why the Red Sox would likely want to bring him back before a playoff series.
Regardless of if that chance to come back before the postseason happens, however, Crochet is confident in himself.
"Someone brought it up the other day. They were like, isn't that crazy? I'm like, not really," Crochet said on Monday. "I mean, not [to be all] me, me, me, me, but I've done crazy things before. I'm not Joe Schmoe. I've done impressive things. I think that that would be a big ask for some people, but I don't think it's a crazy ask for me."
This isn't entirely new territory for Crochet. In 2020, the Chicago White Sox added him to their postseason roster when he had limited time in live action due to the pandemic and coming out of college. He pitched well in that brief opportunity, throwing 0.2 innings with 2 strikeouts.
The Red Sox Postseason Rotation is Up for Debate
Heading into the postseason, pitching is a strength for the Red Sox. Even with injuries, that much has become obvious. Still, questions remain about the actual rotation in the postseason.
Sonny Gray and Payton Tolle will make starts in a three-game series. That's not up for debate. There is debate about which of the two gets Game One. Then, Game Three is going to be between Ranger Suarez and Jake Bennett. The lean there is certainly for the well-paid Suarez, who is a veteran with postseason success. However, stranger things have happened.
Starters who could be coming back from injury, including Houck and Crochet, are going to be seen as relievers. That's presumably how the Red Sox will also continue to use Brayan Bello and Patrick Sandoval.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

One miserable inning was enough to put the Red Sox in a hole. A pair of missed opportunities prevented them from climbing out of it.
Patrick Sandoval endured a brutal 44-pitch second inning in which the Rangers scored four times, and the Red Sox repeatedly came up empty with runners on base in a 4-2 loss Tuesday night at Globe Life Field.
Boston (82-69) opened its final road trip of the regular season with a loss and fell to 7-6 in September. The Red Sox did, however, move another step closer to securing a postseason berth after Toronto was routed by Detroit, reducing Boston’s magic number to five.
Any potential celebration will have to wait until after the Red Sox leave Texas. Even if Boston wins the final two games of the series, Toronto is off Thursday and would remain mathematically alive entering Friday.
Sandoval’s night began when he struck out the first four Rangers he faced before everything unraveled in a second inning that seemed as though it might never end.
With two outs, Brandon Nimmo and Ezequiel Duran delivered hard-hit singles at 106.3 mph and 105.3 mph, respectively. Elias Díaz followed by pulling a two-run double into left field to give Texas a 2-0 lead.
Sandoval never recovered walking former Sox catcher Danny Jansen and Justin Foscue before Corey Seager dropped a bloop single into shallow left, just beyond the reach of Trevor Story, allowing two more runs to score. By the time Sandoval finally escaped, he had thrown 44 pitches in the inning and Boston trailed 4-0.
Sandoval lasted just 2 2/3 innings and saw his ERA climb to 4.99.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
The left-hander’s return from injury provided Boston with some needed innings after he was activated July 9, and he delivered several quality outings along the way. But with the postseason approaching, his place on the October roster has become increasingly uncertain.
Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett are ahead of him in the rotation picture, while Brayan Bello has found success in a bulk role. Garrett Crochet and Tanner Houck are also attempting to return before the postseason.
Patrick Sandoval strikes out the side in the 1st.
Justin Foscue made him throw 9 pitches to start the game. Needed 19 total to finish the inning. pic.twitter.com/qpUpDLA5Rc
Sandoval will have time to try and clean things up, but it’s looking as if the Red Sox are better suited with the lefty as a spectator when they inevitably travel to the Bronx.
Boston’s offense quickly cut the deficit in half against Jacob deGrom.
Nick Sogard jumped on a pitch in the third and sent it down the right-field line for a two-run homer, pulling the Red Sox within 4-2.
Sogard didn’t hit his first major league homer until his 322nd plate appearance Aug. 19. He has now hit five in his last 99 plate appearances, all coming over a 24-game span.
The versatile infielder contributed in other ways, too. Sogard perfectly executed a sacrifice bunt in the fifth to move two runners into scoring position and later made an athletic play to complete a 1-4-3 double play.
But the Red Sox couldn’t capitalize on their opportunities against deGrom. The Texas right-hander held Boston to three hits and struck out eight over five innings while maintaining a fastball around 97 mph.

Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.
